text: Lesson two's plan assumed raw_customers already exists in Snowflake. Something has to put it there first — and that's today's lesson. dbt transforms data that's already in the warehouse; it doesn't load data into the warehouse. That loading step comes first, using the exact same stage-and-COPY INTO pattern from the Snowflake course earlier in this catalog.

First, create a database and schema, then a stage pointing at the real public bucket. This is the actual dbt Labs Jaffle Shop seed data, hosted publicly on S3 — no fabricated sample, no credentials required. Run CREATE OR REPLACE STAGE with that URL, then LIST at-sign jaffle_shop_stage to confirm you really see jaffle_shop_customers.csv, jaffle_shop_orders.csv, and jaffle_shop_payments.csv sitting there. This project only needs the first one.

Next, define a file format — comma-delimited, skip the header row, handle quoted fields — the same options from the Snowflake course's own lab. Then create the target table. The real raw_customers seed has exactly three columns: id, first_name, and last_name. Keep the table that simple because the real data is that simple.

Now load it. COPY INTO raw_customers, from the staged file, using that file format, with ON_ERROR set to CONTINUE. Read the result the same way you learned in the Snowflake course: a status of LOADED, a rows_parsed count, and a rows_loaded count. If those two numbers don't match, check the first_error column before assuming everything's fine. Then run a quick SELECT COUNT and a SELECT star with a LIMIT to eyeball the data.

Notice the sequence: load first, with Snowflake's own tools, then transform, with dbt. Those are two separate jobs. If this loading step were skipped, dbt would have nothing to point at — which is exactly what the next lesson starts setting up.

With raw_customers really sitting in your Snowflake account, the raw side of this project is done. Next lesson, we set up the dbt project itself and connect it to this exact Snowflake account — dbt init, profiles.yml, and the real connection basics.
